clue.text: Opposition policy after local depression is lifted

indicators.note: after means coming later, so the piece named first in the clue goes second in the answer
something lifted is taken away, so a chunk comes out of the word before it

parts.note: a local is someone who lives in the area
a dent is a small hollow or depression in a surface
a stance is a declared position or policy

explanation.surface: A political opposition party announces its policy once a local economic slump has lifted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Depression' reads as an economic slump, but it is a physical hollow, and 'lifted' means removed rather than ended; 'local' is a noun, a person who lives nearby.
explanation.definitionFit: Resistance is the act of pushing back against something, exactly what opposition means as a noun.

clue.text: Vindicates old tradesmen losing weight

indicators.note: to lose something is to be left without it, so a letter goes missing

parts.note: wrights are makers or craftsmen, an old word surviving in wheelwright and playwright
W is the abbreviation for weight

explanation.surface: Old craftsmen are proved right after shedding a few pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: A wright is an old word for a craftsman, still seen in wheelwright and shipwright.
explanation.definitionFit: To right a wrong is to set it straight, so rights works as a verb meaning justifies or clears.

clue.text: Harvester possibly showing rest of snooker

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a harvester or harvestman is a long-legged eight-legged arachnid
second meaning: a cue rest with long curved legs used to reach over other balls

explanation.surface: A combine harvester shows what is left of a snooker game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rest of' looks like 'the remainder of', but a rest is a stick that supports the cue; the snooker version with arched legs has this name.
explanation.definitionFit: Harvestmen are arachnids often called daddy longlegs, loosely grouped with eight-legged web spinners, and the snooker rest shares their long-legged look.

clue.text: Meet entertaining player? Fine

indicators.note: to entertain guests is to take them in, so one word holds another inside it

parts.note: to meet a need or demand is to satisfy it
a player on the stage is an actor

explanation.surface: A host is asked to meet and entertain a sportsman, and agrees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Player' suggests a sportsman, but it is the theatrical sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Fine in the sense of acceptable or good enough is satisfactory, both describing an adequate standard.

clue.text: Relative is very thin, hiding head

indicators.note: with the head hidden, the top letter is out of sight and drops away

parts.note: gaunt means haggard and very thin

explanation.surface: A painfully thin relation hides her face.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down answer the head is the first letter, so G goes.
explanation.definitionFit: An aunt is a parent's sister, one example of a family member or relative.

clue.text: Letters from those against working with soldiers

parts.note: the cons are the arguments or people against, as in pros and cons
a machine that is on is working
soldiers are a caste of ants

explanation.surface: Anti-war campaigners write letters while working alongside the army.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Soldiers' wants to be troops such as OR or TA, but here it means the insects, soldier ants.
explanation.definitionFit: Consonants are all the alphabet characters other than the vowels, so they are a set of letters.

clue.text: Plans putting junk mail on the counter

indicators.note: counter means contrary or opposite in direction, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: spam is unwanted bulk mail, especially email

explanation.surface: Someone schemes by leaving unwanted circulars on a shop counter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the counter' looks like a place to leave post, but counter here means going the opposite way.
explanation.definitionFit: Plans in the sense of drawings of a building or area layout are maps, the nouns being close synonyms.

clue.text: Sporty young fliers keeping lithe somehow

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: the ATC, Air Training Corps, is the RAF youth organisation for cadets

indicators.note: somehow means in some unspecified way, so the letters are put in an unstated order

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Fit young pilots manage to stay supple.
explanation.walkthrough: The Air Training Corps is a British youth organisation for would-be RAF cadets.
explanation.definitionFit: Athletic describes someone fit and fond of physical exercise, a synonym for sporty.

clue.text: Second urine sample is most pleasing

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for second
wee is informal British for urine
a sample is taken for a test

explanation.surface: A patient's second urine sample turns out to be the most agreeable.
explanation.walkthrough: A urine sample is a WEE TEST; wee is a childish British word for urine.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweet means pleasant or agreeable, so its superlative is a synonym for most pleasing.

clue.text: Tap with doubly good plating is shiny

indicators.note: plating is a coat laid all over an object, so letters wrap around the outside of another piece

parts.note: G is the abbreviation for good, used twice
to tap a phone is to listen in on it

explanation.surface: A tap with double-thick good-quality plating gleams.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tap' looks like a plumbing fixture, but it is phone surveillance; one G sits either side of LISTEN IN.
explanation.definitionFit: Glistening describes a surface that shines with reflected light, so it is an adjectival synonym for shiny.

clue.text: Excelled having fired new trainer?

indicators.note: firing someone removes them from the staff, so a letter is dismissed from the word

parts.note: to shine at something is to excel at it
N is the standard abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A sports trainer did brilliantly after sacking the newcomer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trainer' reads as a coach, but the question mark marks it as a sports shoe, one example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A trainer is a sports shoe, so it is an example of footwear, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Release article on part of speech by Bond

parts.note: an is the indefinite article
a noun is one of the grammatical parts of speech
to bond things is to cement them together

explanation.surface: A press release comments on something James Bond said.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital makes Bond look like 007, but it is a binding material.
explanation.definitionFit: A release as in a press release is a public statement, which is an announcement of news.

clue.text: I'm a Believer is number one?

parts.note: number one is 'the first', and this word starts that phrase
first as an ordinal is written 1ST, and the digit 1 is read as the letter I

explanation.surface: The Monkees hit I'm a Believer topped the charts.
explanation.walkthrough: The italics suggest the song title, but only 'Believer' defines; 'number one' is THE 1ST, and the 1 looks just like an I.
explanation.definitionFit: A theist is someone who believes in a god, so the word is a narrower synonym for a religious believer.

clue.text: Former capital site could be Scotland's prettiest

parts.note: Bonn was the capital of West Germany

indicators.note: could be suggests a possible alternative form, so the letters may be put in another order

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A historic capital's location might be the loveliest in Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: Edinburgh wants to be the former capital, but it is Bonn, capital of West Germany until reunification.
explanation.definitionFit: Bonnie is a Scots word meaning pretty or attractive, so the superlative is Scottish for prettiest.

clue.text: Incentive scheme to restrict international levy

indicators.note: restricting something means hemming it in, so one piece is enclosed by another

parts.note: a motion is a formal proposal or scheme put to a meeting
I is the abbreviation for international
VAT is value added tax, a levy on sales

explanation.surface: A government incentive scheme is designed to cap a global tax.
explanation.walkthrough: VAT is value added tax, the British sales tax.
explanation.definitionFit: Motivation is the reason or drive to act, and an incentive is something that provides such a push.

clue.text: Work in Washington with American politicians to create research facilities

parts.note: labor is the American spelling of labour, meaning work
A is a standard abbreviation for American
Tories are members of the British Conservative Party

explanation.surface: American legislators in Washington join forces to set up science labs.
explanation.walkthrough: The American politicians look like one unit, but 'American' is just A and the politicians are British Tories; 'in Washington' asks for the US spelling LABOR.
explanation.definitionFit: Laboratories are the buildings or rooms where scientific experiments and investigation are carried out.

clue.text: West has nothing to swap with America for unexpected event

indicators.note: a swap trades one thing out and puts another in its place

parts.note: the Occident is an old word for the West
O, like zero, stands for nothing
A is an abbreviation for America

explanation.surface: The West has nothing to trade with the USA, an unforeseen turn of events.
explanation.walkthrough: The Occident is the old name for the western world, as the Orient is for the East.
explanation.definitionFit: An accident is something that happens by chance, without plan or warning, hence an unforeseen occurrence.

clue.text: Idiot in football team scoffed, a recent recruit

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece is placed within another

parts.note: a football side has 11 players, and the two digits 1 1 read as two letter Is
nit is British slang for a fool, short for nitwit
to scoff food is to eat it greedily

explanation.surface: A new signing in the football team was mocked as an idiot.
explanation.walkthrough: The team wants to be XI, but it is 11 written with the ones read as Is; 'scoffed' looks like mocked, but it is the British sense of eating greedily.
explanation.definitionFit: An initiate is someone newly admitted to a group or society, so the noun fits a new recruit.

clue.text: Limiting fraud with firm recycling gin

parts.note: a con is a swindle or fraud

indicators.note: recycled material is broken down and remade into something new, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: firm in the sense of strict or unbending
taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A company is cutting down fraud while recycling gin bottles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Firm' reads as a company noun, but it is the adjective STRICT.
explanation.definitionFit: Constricting means squeezing or restricting something, so it is a synonym for limiting as a present participle.

clue.text: Moan about company tax haven

indicators.note: about can mean turned around or in a different arrangement, so the letters are moved

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder
Co is the abbreviation for company

explanation.surface: Someone grumbles about a firm using an offshore tax shelter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' reads as 'concerning', but it asks for a rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Monaco levies no personal income tax on residents, making the Riviera principality a famous place for sheltering wealth.

clue.text: Rank sculptures out of east

indicators.note: one thing out of another has left it, so a letter is removed

parts.note: statues are carved or cast sculptures
E is the abbreviation for east

explanation.surface: Foul-smelling sculptures have been moved out of the eastern gallery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rank' looks like an adjective meaning foul, but it is the noun for standing.
explanation.definitionFit: Status is a person's standing or position in a hierarchy, the same as their rank.

clue.text: Bury — somewhere to go when heading west for a break

parts.note: to inter is to bury a body

indicators.note: in an across answer west is leftward, so moving west means reading right to left

parts.note: the lav is an informal word for the toilet, where one goes

explanation.surface: The Lancashire town of Bury is offered as a destination for a westbound holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: Bury, capitalised, looks like the town in Lancashire, but it is the verb; 'somewhere to go' is the toilet, where one needs to go.
explanation.definitionFit: An interval is a pause, such as the break between acts of a play, so it matches break as a noun.

clue.text: Salesman ought to declare account

parts.note: a rep is a sales representative

indicators.note: declaring something is saying it out loud, so we want a spelling matching the spoken form

parts.note: in a British accent this word rhymes with the spelling ORT

explanation.surface: A travelling salesman should declare his expenses account.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Account' looks like a bank or expenses account, but it is a narrative; the sound of 'ought' is spelt ORT, relying on a non-rhotic accent where the R is silent.
explanation.definitionFit: A report is a spoken or written account of events, so the two nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: Heartlessly charge for toboggan

indicators.note: without a heart means losing the centre, so the middle letter goes

parts.note: a lunge is a sudden forward charge

explanation.surface: Someone cruelly overcharges for hiring a sledge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charge' suggests a price, but it is a sudden rush forward.
explanation.definitionFit: A luge is a small racing sled ridden feet first, so it is a kind of toboggan.

clue.text: Spirit seen in Ireland

indicators.note: something seen inside another thing is contained within it, so the letters lie inside the next word

parts.note: the middle letters of the country's name

explanation.surface: A ghost or a national spirit is spotted in Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirit' tempts a drink like whiskey, but it means verve.
explanation.definitionFit: Elan is dash and energetic flair, the lively quality we call spirit in a person.

clue.text: Leaseholder maybe pursuing place in France for officer

indicators.note: to pursue is to follow behind, so this piece is placed second in the chain

parts.note: lieu is the French word for place
a leaseholder is one kind of tenant, hence maybe

explanation.surface: A leaseholder chases after a French property to hand over to an official.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' signals that a leaseholder is only one example of a tenant.
explanation.definitionFit: A lieutenant is a junior commissioned rank in the army or navy, so it is one kind of officer.

clue.text: Figure dumping husband to see Evergreen?

indicators.note: dumping is getting rid of something, so a letter is thrown out

parts.note: a figure is a numeral, here the number after two
H is the abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: A woman leaves her husband to go and see Evergreen, perhaps a show or a new lover.
explanation.walkthrough: The italics make Evergreen look like a title, but it is a plant that keeps its leaves; the question mark admits that only some trees are evergreen.
explanation.definitionFit: An evergreen such as a pine or holly is often a tree, so the answer is an example-based definition.

clue.text: Aims to switch to the other side of TV, getting fresh ideas

indicators.text: to switch to the other side of TV
indicators.note: moving from one side of a pair to the other swaps its left member for its right member

parts.note: aims are intentions or purposes
the right-hand letter of the pair replaces the left-hand T

explanation.surface: A TV producer's aims are to change channels and come up with new concepts.
explanation.walkthrough: The first T in INTENTIONS crosses over to its partner in TV and becomes V.
explanation.definitionFit: Inventions are original creations or devised novelties, which are new ideas brought into being.
